case_info.scenario: A 62-year-old man presented with progressive lower extremity weakness and involuntary movements. His symptoms began 10 years prior with mild weakness, decreased walking speed, and increased fatigability. Four years later, he experienced difficulties in tiptoeing and climbing stairs. Three years ago, he developed involuntary shoulder shrugging and lip pursing. He denied dysphagia, dysarthria, ptosis, and diplopia and reported no relevant personal or family history. Prior glucocorticoid therapy for diagnosis of polymyositis had yielded no improvement. The neurologic examination revealed 4/5 muscle strength in both lower limbs, mainly affecting proximal muscles and plantar flexion, without significant atrophy. Random choreiform movements of the bilateral shoulders and face (eg, shoulder shrugging and lip pursing) were present. Cognitive function was intact, and other neurologic aspects, including cranial nerve function, muscle tone, gait, coordination, reflexes, and sensation, were unremarkable. Laboratory test results were normal except for elevated creatine kinase (CK; 1961 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (554 U/L). Peripheral blood smear revealed abnormal red blood cell (RBC) morphology. Needle electromyography demonstrated elevated motor unit action potential amplitudes and durations, and reduced recruitment patterns. Muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multifocal hyperintense lesions on T1- and T2-weighted images in the posterior thigh muscles (semimembranosus and biceps femoris), sparing the anterior thigh and adductors (Figure). Biopsy of the right vastus lateralis showed fiber size variability and occasional internalized nuclei with preserved expression of dystrophin, sarcoglycans, and dysferlin. Brain MRI and electrocardiography were unremarkable. Screening for malignancy and systemic disease via cardiac ultrasonography and thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities.
case_info.caption: Axial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thighs revealed hyperintense lesions (arrowheads) within the bilateral thigh muscles, predominantly affecting the posterior compartment.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with progressive lower extremities weakness, choreiform movements, and significantly elevated CK levels. Electromyography revealed chronic neurogenic changes, while muscle MRI indicated a chronic myopathic process or chronic denervation. Muscle biopsy showed nonspecific myopathic features without evidence of inflammatory myopathy (no endomysial or perimysial inflammation), mitochondrial myopathy (no ragged red fibers), or muscular dystrophies (negative immunohistochemistry for common dystrophy-related proteins). These findings suggested both myogenic and neurogenic involvement. Notably, the detection of acanthocytes in the peripheral blood provided a crucial diagnostic clue. Whole exome sequencing confirmed a hemizygous pathogenic variant in theXKgene (c.265del, p.Ile89Serfs*41), establishing a diagnosis of McLeod syndrome (MLS). MLS is an extremely rare, progressive, X-linked recessive neuroacanthocytosis first reported by Allen et al1in 1961. It is a multisystem disorder affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and neuromuscular, cardiovascular, and hematological systems.2MLS is caused by variants in theXKgene, which encodes the XK protein responsible for presenting the Kx blood group antigen on RBCs. The XK protein plays pivotal roles in organogenesis, cellular structure, and nutrient exchanges.3Its deficiency leads to erythrocyte acanthocytosis, chronic hemolysis, and degeneration of neurons and muscle fibers. Alloantibodies within the Kell and Kx blood group system can induce severe transfusion reactions and significant anemia.4Neurologically, MLS shares clinical similarities with Huntington disease (HD), including chorea, psychiatric disturbances, cognitive decline, and seizures.4,5Neuromuscular manifestations often include axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, neurogenic atrophy, and myopathy.2,6Additionally, cardiac abnormalities, such as dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, are common and may lead to sudden death.7The multisystem nature of MLS necessitates a broad differential diagnosis. Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc), another neuroacanthocytosis syndrome, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused byVPS13Agene variants. Compared to MLS, ChAc typically presents earlier in adulthood and is characterized by oromandibular chorea, parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric problems, diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, and seizures. However, cardiac involvement is uncommon.3While the disorders share common features, such as acanthocytes and chorea, key distinguishing characteristics of MLS include later onset, X-linked inheritance, and prominent cardiac manifestations.8In this patient, the later age at onset and lack of characteristic orofacial dyskinesias make ChAc less likely. HD is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by the expansion of CAG repeats in theHTTgene.9Its hallmark features—chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and progressive cognitive decline—can overlap with MLS. However, HD is usually associated with characteristic caudate atrophy and ventricular enlargement on brain imaging, which were absent in this case. Moreover, HD lacks CK elevation and acanthocytosis, and the patient’s inheritance pattern did not support this diagnosis. Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism that can cause hepatic, ocular, and neurologic abnormalities. Neurological manifestations also include parkinsonism, chorea, athetosis, and psychiatric disturbance.10In this patient, despite the presence of choreiform symptoms, the distinct pattern of inheritance, elevated CK levels, normal ceruloplasmin levels, absence of hepatic involvement, and unremarkable brain MRI findings collectively excluded this diagnosis. Currently, the management of MLS primarily focuses on symptomatic and individualized treatment. In this patient, tiapride was prescribed to alleviate chorea symptoms, resulting in modest improvement. Although no cardiac abnormalities were present, regular surveillance with electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and cardiac biomarkers is essential due to the risk of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. When transfusions are needed, Kx-negative blood must be used to prevent alloimmunization. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient’s involuntary movements had slightly improved, but muscle weakness persisted without progression, and cardiac assessment remained normal. In summary, this case underscores that MLS is a complex multisystem disorder affecting neuromuscular, hematologic, cardiovascular and CNS functions. Acanthocytes in peripheral blood provides key diagnosis clues. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Axial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thighs revealed hyperintense lesions (arrowheads) within the bilateral thigh muscles, predominantly affecting the posterior compartment.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with progressive lower extremities weakness, choreiform movements, and significantly elevated CK levels. Electromyography revealed chronic neurogenic changes, while muscle MRI indicated a chronic myopathic process or chronic denervation. Muscle biopsy showed nonspecific myopathic features without evidence of inflammatory myopathy (no endomysial or perimysial inflammation), mitochondrial myopathy (no ragged red fibers), or muscular dystrophies (negative immunohistochemistry for common dystrophy-related proteins). These findings suggested both myogenic and neurogenic involvement. Notably, the detection of acanthocytes in the peripheral blood provided a crucial diagnostic clue. Whole exome sequencing confirmed a hemizygous pathogenic variant in theXKgene (c.265del, p.Ile89Serfs*41), establishing a diagnosis of McLeod syndrome (MLS). MLS is an extremely rare, progressive, X-linked recessive neuroacanthocytosis first reported by Allen et al1in 1961. It is a multisystem disorder affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and neuromuscular, cardiovascular, and hematological systems.2MLS is caused by variants in theXKgene, which encodes the XK protein responsible for presenting the Kx blood group antigen on RBCs. The XK protein plays pivotal roles in organogenesis, cellular structure, and nutrient exchanges.3Its deficiency leads to erythrocyte acanthocytosis, chronic hemolysis, and degeneration of neurons and muscle fibers. Alloantibodies within the Kell and Kx blood group system can induce severe transfusion reactions and significant anemia.4Neurologically, MLS shares clinical similarities with Huntington disease (HD), including chorea, psychiatric disturbances, cognitive decline, and seizures.4,5Neuromuscular manifestations often include axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, neurogenic atrophy, and myopathy.2,6Additionally, cardiac abnormalities, such as dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, are common and may lead to sudden death.7The multisystem nature of MLS necessitates a broad differential diagnosis. Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc), another neuroacanthocytosis syndrome, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused byVPS13Agene variants. Compared to MLS, ChAc typically presents earlier in adulthood and is characterized by oromandibular chorea, parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric problems, diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, and seizures. However, cardiac involvement is uncommon.3While the disorders share common features, such as acanthocytes and chorea, key distinguishing characteristics of MLS include later onset, X-linked inheritance, and prominent cardiac manifestations.8In this patient, the later age at onset and lack of characteristic orofacial dyskinesias make ChAc less likely. HD is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by the expansion of CAG repeats in theHTTgene.9Its hallmark features—chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and progressive cognitive decline—can overlap with MLS. However, HD is usually associated with characteristic caudate atrophy and ventricular enlargement on brain imaging, which were absent in this case. Moreover, HD lacks CK elevation and acanthocytosis, and the patient’s inheritance pattern did not support this diagnosis. Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism that can cause hepatic, ocular, and neurologic abnormalities. Neurological manifestations also include parkinsonism, chorea, athetosis, and psychiatric disturbance.10In this patient, despite the presence of choreiform symptoms, the distinct pattern of inheritance, elevated CK levels, normal ceruloplasmin levels, absence of hepatic involvement, and unremarkable brain MRI findings collectively excluded this diagnosis. Currently, the management of MLS primarily focuses on symptomatic and individualized treatment. In this patient, tiapride was prescribed to alleviate chorea symptoms, resulting in modest improvement. Although no cardiac abnormalities were present, regular surveillance with electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and cardiac biomarkers is essential due to the risk of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. When transfusions are needed, Kx-negative blood must be used to prevent alloimmunization. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient’s involuntary movements had slightly improved, but muscle weakness persisted without progression, and cardiac assessment remained normal. In summary, this case underscores that MLS is a complex multisystem disorder affecting neuromuscular, hematologic, cardiovascular and CNS functions. Acanthocytes in peripheral blood provides key diagnosis clues. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.caption: Axial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thighs revealed hyperintense lesions (arrowheads) within the bilateral thigh muscles, predominantly affecting the posterior compartment.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with progressive lower extremities weakness, choreiform movements, and significantly elevated CK levels. Electromyography revealed chronic neurogenic changes, while muscle MRI indicated a chronic myopathic process or chronic denervation. Muscle biopsy showed nonspecific myopathic features without evidence of inflammatory myopathy (no endomysial or perimysial inflammation), mitochondrial myopathy (no ragged red fibers), or muscular dystrophies (negative immunohistochemistry for common dystrophy-related proteins). These findings suggested both myogenic and neurogenic involvement. Notably, the detection of acanthocytes in the peripheral blood provided a crucial diagnostic clue. Whole exome sequencing confirmed a hemizygous pathogenic variant in theXKgene (c.265del, p.Ile89Serfs*41), establishing a diagnosis of McLeod syndrome (MLS). MLS is an extremely rare, progressive, X-linked recessive neuroacanthocytosis first reported by Allen et al1in 1961. It is a multisystem disorder affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and neuromuscular, cardiovascular, and hematological systems.2MLS is caused by variants in theXKgene, which encodes the XK protein responsible for presenting the Kx blood group antigen on RBCs. The XK protein plays pivotal roles in organogenesis, cellular structure, and nutrient exchanges.3Its deficiency leads to erythrocyte acanthocytosis, chronic hemolysis, and degeneration of neurons and muscle fibers. Alloantibodies within the Kell and Kx blood group system can induce severe transfusion reactions and significant anemia.4Neurologically, MLS shares clinical similarities with Huntington disease (HD), including chorea, psychiatric disturbances, cognitive decline, and seizures.4,5Neuromuscular manifestations often include axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, neurogenic atrophy, and myopathy.2,6Additionally, cardiac abnormalities, such as dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, are common and may lead to sudden death.7The multisystem nature of MLS necessitates a broad differential diagnosis. Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc), another neuroacanthocytosis syndrome, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused byVPS13Agene variants. Compared to MLS, ChAc typically presents earlier in adulthood and is characterized by oromandibular chorea, parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric problems, diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, and seizures. However, cardiac involvement is uncommon.3While the disorders share common features, such as acanthocytes and chorea, key distinguishing characteristics of MLS include later onset, X-linked inheritance, and prominent cardiac manifestations.8In this patient, the later age at onset and lack of characteristic orofacial dyskinesias make ChAc less likely. HD is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by the expansion of CAG repeats in theHTTgene.9Its hallmark features—chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and progressive cognitive decline—can overlap with MLS. However, HD is usually associated with characteristic caudate atrophy and ventricular enlargement on brain imaging, which were absent in this case. Moreover, HD lacks CK elevation and acanthocytosis, and the patient’s inheritance pattern did not support this diagnosis. Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism that can cause hepatic, ocular, and neurologic abnormalities. Neurological manifestations also include parkinsonism, chorea, athetosis, and psychiatric disturbance.10In this patient, despite the presence of choreiform symptoms, the distinct pattern of inheritance, elevated CK levels, normal ceruloplasmin levels, absence of hepatic involvement, and unremarkable brain MRI findings collectively excluded this diagnosis. Currently, the management of MLS primarily focuses on symptomatic and individualized treatment. In this patient, tiapride was prescribed to alleviate chorea symptoms, resulting in modest improvement. Although no cardiac abnormalities were present, regular surveillance with electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and cardiac biomarkers is essential due to the risk of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. When transfusions are needed, Kx-negative blood must be used to prevent alloimmunization. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient’s involuntary movements had slightly improved, but muscle weakness persisted without progression, and cardiac assessment remained normal. In summary, this case underscores that MLS is a complex multisystem disorder affecting neuromuscular, hematologic, cardiovascular and CNS functions. Acanthocytes in peripheral blood provides key diagnosis clues. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

case_info.explanation: This patient presented with progressive lower extremities weakness, choreiform movements, and significantly elevated CK levels. Electromyography revealed chronic neurogenic changes, while muscle MRI indicated a chronic myopathic process or chronic denervation. Muscle biopsy showed nonspecific myopathic features without evidence of inflammatory myopathy (no endomysial or perimysial inflammation), mitochondrial myopathy (no ragged red fibers), or muscular dystrophies (negative immunohistochemistry for common dystrophy-related proteins). These findings suggested both myogenic and neurogenic involvement. Notably, the detection of acanthocytes in the peripheral blood provided a crucial diagnostic clue. Whole exome sequencing confirmed a hemizygous pathogenic variant in theXKgene (c.265del, p.Ile89Serfs*41), establishing a diagnosis of McLeod syndrome (MLS). MLS is an extremely rare, progressive, X-linked recessive neuroacanthocytosis first reported by Allen et al1in 1961. It is a multisystem disorder affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and neuromuscular, cardiovascular, and hematological systems.2MLS is caused by variants in theXKgene, which encodes the XK protein responsible for presenting the Kx blood group antigen on RBCs. The XK protein plays pivotal roles in organogenesis, cellular structure, and nutrient exchanges.3Its deficiency leads to erythrocyte acanthocytosis, chronic hemolysis, and degeneration of neurons and muscle fibers. Alloantibodies within the Kell and Kx blood group system can induce severe transfusion reactions and significant anemia.4Neurologically, MLS shares clinical similarities with Huntington disease (HD), including chorea, psychiatric disturbances, cognitive decline, and seizures.4,5Neuromuscular manifestations often include axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, neurogenic atrophy, and myopathy.2,6Additionally, cardiac abnormalities, such as dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, are common and may lead to sudden death.7The multisystem nature of MLS necessitates a broad differential diagnosis. Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc), another neuroacanthocytosis syndrome, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused byVPS13Agene variants. Compared to MLS, ChAc typically presents earlier in adulthood and is characterized by oromandibular chorea, parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric problems, diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, and seizures. However, cardiac involvement is uncommon.3While the disorders share common features, such as acanthocytes and chorea, key distinguishing characteristics of MLS include later onset, X-linked inheritance, and prominent cardiac manifestations.8In this patient, the later age at onset and lack of characteristic orofacial dyskinesias make ChAc less likely. HD is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by the expansion of CAG repeats in theHTTgene.9Its hallmark features—chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and progressive cognitive decline—can overlap with MLS. However, HD is usually associated with characteristic caudate atrophy and ventricular enlargement on brain imaging, which were absent in this case. Moreover, HD lacks CK elevation and acanthocytosis, and the patient’s inheritance pattern did not support this diagnosis. Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism that can cause hepatic, ocular, and neurologic abnormalities. Neurological manifestations also include parkinsonism, chorea, athetosis, and psychiatric disturbance.10In this patient, despite the presence of choreiform symptoms, the distinct pattern of inheritance, elevated CK levels, normal ceruloplasmin levels, absence of hepatic involvement, and unremarkable brain MRI findings collectively excluded this diagnosis. Currently, the management of MLS primarily focuses on symptomatic and individualized treatment. In this patient, tiapride was prescribed to alleviate chorea symptoms, resulting in modest improvement. Although no cardiac abnormalities were present, regular surveillance with electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and cardiac biomarkers is essential due to the risk of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. When transfusions are needed, Kx-negative blood must be used to prevent alloimmunization. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient’s involuntary movements had slightly improved, but muscle weakness persisted without progression, and cardiac assessment remained normal. In summary, this case underscores that MLS is a complex multisystem disorder affecting neuromuscular, hematologic, cardiovascular and CNS functions. Acanthocytes in peripheral blood provides key diagnosis clues. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 62-year-old man presented with progressive lower extremity weakness and involuntary movements. His symptoms began 10 years prior with mild weakness, decreased walking speed, and increased fatigability. Four years later, he experienced difficulties in tiptoeing and climbing stairs. Three years ago, he developed involuntary shoulder shrugging and lip pursing. He denied dysphagia, dysarthria, ptosis, and diplopia and reported no relevant personal or family history. Prior glucocorticoid therapy for diagnosis of polymyositis had yielded no improvement. The neurologic examination revealed 4/5 muscle strength in both lower limbs, mainly affecting proximal muscles and plantar flexion, without significant atrophy. Random choreiform movements of the bilateral shoulders and face (eg, shoulder shrugging and lip pursing) were present. Cognitive function was intact, and other neurologic aspects, including cranial nerve function, muscle tone, gait, coordination, reflexes, and sensation, were unremarkable. Laboratory test results were normal except for elevated creatine kinase (CK; 1961 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (554 U/L). Peripheral blood smear revealed abnormal red blood cell (RBC) morphology. Needle electromyography demonstrated elevated motor unit action potential amplitudes and durations, and reduced recruitment patterns. Muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multifocal hyperintense lesions on T1- and T2-weighted images in the posterior thigh muscles (semimembranosus and biceps femoris), sparing the anterior thigh and adductors (Figure). Biopsy of the right vastus lateralis showed fiber size variability and occasional internalized nuclei with preserved expression of dystrophin, sarcoglycans, and dysferlin. Brain MRI and electrocardiography were unremarkable. Screening for malignancy and systemic disease via cardiac ultrasonography and thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",

    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",

    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"

The involuntary movements and elevated CK levels are particularly suggestive of this condition, making it the most appropriate next step in management.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: This patient presented with progressive lower extremities weakness, choreiform movements, and significantly elevated CK levels. Electromyography revealed chronic neurogenic changes, while muscle MRI indicated a chronic myopathic process or chronic denervation. Muscle biopsy showed nonspecific myopathic features without evidence of inflammatory myopathy (no endomysial or perimysial inflammation), mitochondrial myopathy (no ragged red fibers), or muscular dystrophies (negative immunohistochemistry for common dystrophy-related proteins). These findings suggested both myogenic and neurogenic involvement. Notably, the detection of acanthocytes in the peripheral blood provided a crucial diagnostic clue. Whole exome sequencing confirmed a hemizygous pathogenic variant in theXKgene (c.265del, p.Ile89Serfs*41), establishing a diagnosis of McLeod syndrome (MLS). MLS is an extremely rare, progressive, X-linked recessive neuroacanthocytosis first reported by Allen et al1in 1961. It is a multisystem disorder affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and neuromuscular, cardiovascular, and hematological systems.2MLS is caused by variants in theXKgene, which encodes the XK protein responsible for presenting the Kx blood group antigen on RBCs. The XK protein plays pivotal roles in organogenesis, cellular structure, and nutrient exchanges.3Its deficiency leads to erythrocyte acanthocytosis, chronic hemolysis, and degeneration of neurons and muscle fibers. Alloantibodies within the Kell and Kx blood group system can induce severe transfusion reactions and significant anemia.4Neurologically, MLS shares clinical similarities with Huntington disease (HD), including chorea, psychiatric disturbances, cognitive decline, and seizures.4,5Neuromuscular manifestations often include axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, neurogenic atrophy, and myopathy.2,6Additionally, cardiac abnormalities, such as dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, are common and may lead to sudden death.7The multisystem nature of MLS necessitates a broad differential diagnosis. Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc), another neuroacanthocytosis syndrome, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused byVPS13Agene variants. Compared to MLS, ChAc typically presents earlier in adulthood and is characterized by oromandibular chorea, parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric problems, diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, and seizures. However, cardiac involvement is uncommon.3While the disorders share common features, such as acanthocytes and chorea, key distinguishing characteristics of MLS include later onset, X-linked inheritance, and prominent cardiac manifestations.8In this patient, the later age at onset and lack of characteristic orofacial dyskinesias make ChAc less likely. HD is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by the expansion of CAG repeats in theHTTgene.9Its hallmark features—chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and progressive cognitive decline—can overlap with MLS. However, HD is usually associated with characteristic caudate atrophy and ventricular enlargement on brain imaging, which were absent in this case. Moreover, HD lacks CK elevation and acanthocytosis, and the patient’s inheritance pattern did not support this diagnosis. Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism that can cause hepatic, ocular, and neurologic abnormalities. Neurological manifestations also include parkinsonism, chorea, athetosis, and psychiatric disturbance.10In this patient, despite the presence of choreiform symptoms, the distinct pattern of inheritance, elevated CK levels, normal ceruloplasmin levels, absence of hepatic involvement, and unremarkable brain MRI findings collectively excluded this diagnosis. Currently, the management of MLS primarily focuses on symptomatic and individualized treatment. In this patient, tiapride was prescribed to alleviate chorea symptoms, resulting in modest improvement. Although no cardiac abnormalities were present, regular surveillance with electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and cardiac biomarkers is essential due to the risk of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. When transfusions are needed, Kx-negative blood must be used to prevent alloimmunization. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient’s involuntary movements had slightly improved, but muscle weakness persisted without progression, and cardiac assessment remained normal. In summary, this case underscores that MLS is a complex multisystem disorder affecting neuromuscular, hematologic, cardiovascular and CNS functions. Acanthocytes in peripheral blood provides key diagnosis clues. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

case_info.caption: Axial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thighs revealed hyperintense lesions (arrowheads) within the bilateral thigh muscles, predominantly affecting the posterior compartment.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with progressive lower extremities weakness, choreiform movements, and significantly elevated CK levels. Electromyography revealed chronic neurogenic changes, while muscle MRI indicated a chronic myopathic process or chronic denervation. Muscle biopsy showed nonspecific myopathic features without evidence of inflammatory myopathy (no endomysial or perimysial inflammation), mitochondrial myopathy (no ragged red fibers), or muscular dystrophies (negative immunohistochemistry for common dystrophy-related proteins). These findings suggested both myogenic and neurogenic involvement. Notably, the detection of acanthocytes in the peripheral blood provided a crucial diagnostic clue. Whole exome sequencing confirmed a hemizygous pathogenic variant in theXKgene (c.265del, p.Ile89Serfs*41), establishing a diagnosis of McLeod syndrome (MLS). MLS is an extremely rare, progressive, X-linked recessive neuroacanthocytosis first reported by Allen et al1in 1961. It is a multisystem disorder affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and neuromuscular, cardiovascular, and hematological systems.2MLS is caused by variants in theXKgene, which encodes the XK protein responsible for presenting the Kx blood group antigen on RBCs. The XK protein plays pivotal roles in organogenesis, cellular structure, and nutrient exchanges.3Its deficiency leads to erythrocyte acanthocytosis, chronic hemolysis, and degeneration of neurons and muscle fibers. Alloantibodies within the Kell and Kx blood group system can induce severe transfusion reactions and significant anemia.4Neurologically, MLS shares clinical similarities with Huntington disease (HD), including chorea, psychiatric disturbances, cognitive decline, and seizures.4,5Neuromuscular manifestations often include axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, neurogenic atrophy, and myopathy.2,6Additionally, cardiac abnormalities, such as dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, are common and may lead to sudden death.7The multisystem nature of MLS necessitates a broad differential diagnosis. Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc), another neuroacanthocytosis syndrome, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused byVPS13Agene variants. Compared to MLS, ChAc typically presents earlier in adulthood and is characterized by oromandibular chorea, parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric problems, diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, and seizures. However, cardiac involvement is uncommon.3While the disorders share common features, such as acanthocytes and chorea, key distinguishing characteristics of MLS include later onset, X-linked inheritance, and prominent cardiac manifestations.8In this patient, the later age at onset and lack of characteristic orofacial dyskinesias make ChAc less likely. HD is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by the expansion of CAG repeats in theHTTgene.9Its hallmark features—chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and progressive cognitive decline—can overlap with MLS. However, HD is usually associated with characteristic caudate atrophy and ventricular enlargement on brain imaging, which were absent in this case. Moreover, HD lacks CK elevation and acanthocytosis, and the patient’s inheritance pattern did not support this diagnosis. Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism that can cause hepatic, ocular, and neurologic abnormalities. Neurological manifestations also include parkinsonism, chorea, athetosis, and psychiatric disturbance.10In this patient, despite the presence of choreiform symptoms, the distinct pattern of inheritance, elevated CK levels, normal ceruloplasmin levels, absence of hepatic involvement, and unremarkable brain MRI findings collectively excluded this diagnosis. Currently, the management of MLS primarily focuses on symptomatic and individualized treatment. In this patient, tiapride was prescribed to alleviate chorea symptoms, resulting in modest improvement. Although no cardiac abnormalities were present, regular surveillance with electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and cardiac biomarkers is essential due to the risk of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. When transfusions are needed, Kx-negative blood must be used to prevent alloimmunization. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient’s involuntary movements had slightly improved, but muscle weakness persisted without progression, and cardiac assessment remained normal. In summary, this case underscores that MLS is a complex multisystem disorder affecting neuromuscular, hematologic, cardiovascular and CNS functions. [NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.caption: Axial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thighs revealed hyperintense lesions (arrowheads) within the bilateral thigh muscles, predominantly affecting the posterior compartment.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with progressive lower extremities weakness, choreiform movements, and significantly elevated CK levels. Electromyography revealed chronic neurogenic changes, while muscle MRI indicated a chronic myopathic process or chronic denervation. Muscle biopsy showed nonspecific myopathic features without evidence of inflammatory myopathy (no endomysial or perimysial inflammation), mitochondrial myopathy (no ragged red fibers), or muscular dystrophies (negative immunohistochemistry for common dystrophy-related proteins). These findings suggested both myogenic and neurogenic involvement. Notably, the detection of acanthocytes in the peripheral blood provided a crucial diagnostic clue. Whole exome sequencing confirmed a hemizygous pathogenic variant in theXKgene (c.265del, p.Ile89Serfs*41), establishing a diagnosis of McLeod syndrome (MLS). MLS is an extremely rare, progressive, X-linked recessive neuroacanthocytosis first reported by Allen et al1in 1961. It is a multisystem disorder affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and neuromuscular, cardiovascular, and hematological systems.2MLS is caused by variants in theXKgene, which encodes the XK protein responsible for presenting the Kx blood group antigen on RBCs. The XK protein plays pivotal roles in organogenesis, cellular structure, and nutrient exchanges.3Its deficiency leads to erythrocyte acanthocytosis, chronic hemolysis, and degeneration of neurons and muscle fibers. Alloantibodies within the Kell and Kx blood group system can induce severe transfusion reactions and significant anemia.4Neurologically, MLS shares clinical similarities with Huntington disease (HD), including chorea, psychiatric disturbances, cognitive decline, and seizures.4,5Neuromuscular manifestations often include axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, neurogenic atrophy, and myopathy.2,6Additionally, cardiac abnormalities, such as dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, are common and may lead to sudden death.7The multisystem nature of MLS necessitates a broad differential diagnosis. Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc), another neuroacanthocytosis syndrome, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused byVPS13Agene variants. Compared to MLS, ChAc typically presents earlier in adulthood and is characterized by oromandibular chorea, parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric problems, diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, and seizures. However, cardiac involvement is uncommon.3While the disorders share common features, such as acanthocytes and chorea, key distinguishing characteristics of MLS include later onset, X-linked inheritance, and prominent cardiac manifestations.8In this patient, the later age at onset and lack of characteristic orofacial dyskinesias make ChAc less likely. HD is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by the expansion of CAG repeats in theHTTgene.9Its hallmark features—chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and progressive cognitive decline—can overlap with MLS. However, HD is usually associated with characteristic caudate atrophy and ventricular enlargement on brain imaging, which were absent in this case. Moreover, HD lacks CK elevation and acanthocytosis, and the patient’s inheritance pattern did not support this diagnosis. Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism that can cause hepatic, ocular, and neurologic abnormalities. Neurological manifestations also include parkinsonism, chorea, athetosis, and psychiatric disturbance.10In this patient, despite the presence of choreiform symptoms, the distinct pattern of inheritance, elevated CK levels, normal ceruloplasmin levels, absence of hepatic involvement, and unremarkable brain MRI findings collectively excluded this diagnosis. Currently, the management of MLS primarily focuses on symptomatic and individualized treatment. In this patient, tiapride was prescribed to alleviate chorea symptoms, resulting in modest improvement. Although no cardiac abnormalities were present, regular surveillance with electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and cardiac biomarkers is essential due to the risk of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. When transfusions are needed, Kx-negative blood must be used to prevent alloimmunization. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient’s involuntary movements had slightly improved, but muscle weakness persisted without progression, and cardiac assessment remained normal. In summary, this case underscores that MLS is a complex multisystem disorder affecting neuromuscular, hematologic, cardiovascular and CNS functions. Acanthocytes in peripheral blood provides key diagnosis clues. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

4. Frustration

case_info.caption: Axial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thighs revealed hyperintense lesions (arrowheads) within the bilateral thigh muscles, predominantly affecting the posterior compartment.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented with progressive lower extremities weakness, choreiform movements, and significantly elevated CK levels. Electromyography revealed chronic neurogenic changes, while muscle MRI indicated a chronic myopathic process or chronic denervation. Muscle biopsy showed nonspecific myopathic features without evidence of inflammatory myopathy (no endomysial or perimysial inflammation), mitochondrial myopathy (no ragged red fibers), or muscular dystrophies (negative immunohistochemistry for common dystrophy-related proteins). These findings suggested both myogenic and neurogenic involvement. Notably, the detection of acanthocytes in the peripheral blood provided a crucial diagnostic clue. Whole exome sequencing confirmed a hemizygous pathogenic variant in theXKgene (c.265del, p.Ile89Serfs*41), establishing a diagnosis of McLeod syndrome (MLS). MLS is an extremely rare, progressive, X-linked recessive neuroacanthocytosis first reported by Allen et al1in 1961. It is a multisystem disorder affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and neuromuscular, cardiovascular, and hematological systems.2MLS is caused by variants in theXKgene, which encodes the XK protein responsible for presenting the Kx blood group antigen on RBCs. The XK protein plays pivotal roles in organogenesis, cellular structure, and nutrient exchanges.3Its deficiency leads to erythrocyte acanthocytosis, chronic hemolysis, and degeneration of neurons and muscle fibers. Alloantibodies within the Kell and Kx blood group system can induce severe transfusion reactions and significant anemia.4Neurologically, MLS shares clinical similarities with Huntington disease (HD), including chorea, psychiatric disturbances, cognitive decline, and seizures.4,5Neuromuscular manifestations often include axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, neurogenic atrophy, and myopathy.2,6Additionally, cardiac abnormalities, such as dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, are common and may lead to sudden death.7The multisystem nature of MLS necessitates a broad differential diagnosis. Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc), another neuroacanthocytosis syndrome, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused byVPS13Agene variants. Compared to MLS, ChAc typically presents earlier in adulthood and is characterized by oromandibular chorea, parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric problems, diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, and seizures. However, cardiac involvement is uncommon.3While the disorders share common features, such as acanthocytes and chorea, key distinguishing characteristics of MLS include later onset, X-linked inheritance, and prominent cardiac manifestations.8In this patient, the later age at onset and lack of characteristic orofacial dyskinesias make ChAc less likely. HD is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by the expansion of CAG repeats in theHTTgene.9Its hallmark features—chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and progressive cognitive decline—can overlap with MLS. However, HD is usually associated with characteristic caudate atrophy and ventricular enlargement on brain imaging, which were absent in this case. Moreover, HD lacks CK elevation and acanthocytosis, and the patient’s inheritance pattern did not support this diagnosis. Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism that can cause hepatic, ocular, and neurologic abnormalities. Neurological manifestations also include parkinsonism, chorea, athetosis, and psychiatric disturbance.10In this patient, despite the presence of choreiform symptoms, the distinct pattern of inheritance, elevated CK levels, normal ceruloplasmin levels, absence of hepatic involvement, and unremarkable brain MRI findings collectively excluded this diagnosis. Currently, the management of MLS primarily focuses on symptomatic and individualized treatment. In this patient, tiapride was prescribed to alleviate chorea symptoms, resulting in modest improvement. Although no cardiac abnormalities were present, regular surveillance with electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and cardiac biomarkers is essential due to the risk of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. When transfusions are needed, Kx-negative blood must be used to prevent alloimmunization. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient’s involuntary movements had slightly improved, but muscle weakness persisted without progression, and cardiac assessment remained normal. In summary, this case underscores that MLS is a complex multisystem disorder affecting neuromuscular, hematologic, cardiovascular and CNS functions. Acanthocytes in peripheral blood provides key diagnosis clues. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
